item.title: Boosting Papers and Reading Guide
item.description:
Boosting Papers and Reading Guide

Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

Boosting is one of the most classic and most practical techniques in machine learning, and its literature spans more than three decades — from the theoretical foundations of the mid-1990s, through the engineering explosion of the 2010s, to industrial deployment in the 2020s — forming a remarkably rich body of knowledge. This article doesn’t just list references; it aims to give readers a clear reading path so they can build their own understanding efficiently, whatever their background.

item.title: Boosting in Python: Classification and Regression
item.description:
Boosting in Python: Classification and Regression

Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

This article provides complete, runnable Python examples covering binary classification, regression, model persistence and SHAP explanation. The code targets sklearn 1.4+, XGBoost 2.1+, LightGBM 4.0+ and CatBoost 1.2+, and includes comments; it has been run end to end under scikit-learn 1.9.1, XGBoost 3.4.1, LightGBM 4.7.0, CatBoost 1.2.10, shap 0.54.1 and optuna 5.1.0 (Python 3.13).

Version differences to watch

  • XGBoost: early_stopping_rounds, eval_metric and callbacks were deprecated in fit() from 1.6 and removed from fit() in 2.1, so they belong in the constructor (the code here follows that).
  • LightGBM: from 4.0, fit() / train() no longer accept early_stopping_rounds or verbose_eval; use callbacks=[lgb.early_stopping(...)] instead. From 4.7 the sklearn interface gains eval_X / eval_y and marks eval_set deprecated (it still works, with a warning).
  • scikit-learn: AdaBoostClassifier’s SAMME.R was deprecated in 1.4 and removed in 1.6; the algorithm parameter itself was deprecated in 1.6 and removed in 1.8, so passing algorithm=... raises TypeError in new versions.

11.1 A complete binary classification workflow

This example uses sklearn’s make_classification to generate data and walks through the whole path from loading to evaluation and visualization, comparing XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost along the way.

item.title: Tuning Boosting Models
item.description:
Tuning Boosting Models

Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

Boosting performance depends heavily on hyperparameters. Unlike random forests, which work out of the box, boosting’s default settings tend to be aggressive (XGBoost’s max_depth=6, eta=0.3), and getting the best out of it takes systematic tuning. This article lays out a general staged tuning framework, gives concrete parameter advice for each algorithm, and offers fixes for the common traps.

10.1 A general strategy: staged tuning

Boosting has many parameters that interact (the learning_rate/n_estimators trade-off, for one). A blind full grid search is both expensive and prone to landing in a local optimum. Staged tuning — layering the work by importance, refining step by step — works better.

Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

The boosting family is crowded — from classic AdaBoost to modern XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost — and each member has its own design philosophy, optimization target and sweet spot. On real projects, picking the right algorithm often matters more than fine-tuning it. This article compares the five mainstream boosting algorithms across several dimensions and lays out a practical decision procedure.

item.title: CatBoost
item.description:
CatBoost

Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

8.1 Overview and core innovations

CatBoost (Categorical Boosting) is a gradient boosted decision tree implementation open-sourced by Yandex, the Russian search company, in 2017. Two papers are central: Prokhorenkova et al., CatBoost: unbiased boosting with categorical features (NeurIPS 2018, arXiv 2017), which introduces ordered boosting and ordered target statistics; and Dorogush, Ershov and Gulin, CatBoost: gradient boosting with categorical features support (arXiv 2018), which covers the library’s overall design, feature combinations and GPU implementation. The name states the positioning: unbiased, efficient gradient boosting for datasets with many categorical features. Compared with XGBoost and LightGBM, CatBoost’s distinctiveness lies in systematically solving, at the theoretical level, the prediction shift problem in gradient boosting, and in proposing ordered boosting and ordered target statistics, with oblivious trees as base learners.

item.title: LightGBM
item.description:
LightGBM

Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

7.1 Overview and core innovations

LightGBM (Light Gradient Boosting Machine) is a highly efficient gradient boosted decision tree system from Guolin Ke and colleagues at Microsoft Research Asia, working with Peking University, published at NIPS 2017 (now NeurIPS; paper LightGBM: A Highly Efficient Gradient Boosting Decision Tree). The next milestone after XGBoost, LightGBM not only speeds up training by orders of magnitude but also shows clear advantages in memory efficiency, high-dimensional sparse data and large-scale settings.

item.title: XGBoost
item.description:
XGBoost

Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

6.1 Overview and core innovations

XGBoost (eXtreme Gradient Boosting) is a scalable end-to-end tree boosting system introduced by Tianqi Chen and Carlos Guestrin at ACM SIGKDD in 2016 (KDD 2016, paper XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System). It reworks gradient boosted decision trees (GBDT) on both the algorithmic and the engineering side, combining second-order Taylor expansion, an explicitly regularized objective, weighted quantile sketches, sparsity-aware split finding and system-level optimizations (block structure, cache awareness, out-of-core computation) to break new ground in both speed and accuracy.

item.title: Boosting Foundations: Additive Models and Loss Functions
item.description:
Boosting Foundations: Additive Models and Loss Functions

Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

3.1 The additive model: boosting’s mathematical base

The mathematical framework of boosting rests on the additive model. An additive model writes a complicated prediction function as a linear combination of simple basis functions, which turns one high-dimensional optimization problem into a series of low-dimensional ones.

3.1.1 The form of an additive model

The general form is

$$f(x) = \sum_{m=1}^M \beta_m b(x; \gamma_m)$$

Notation:

Symbol Meaning Notes
$x$ Input feature vector $x \in \mathbb{R}^d$
$M$ Total number of basis functions Corresponds to the number of boosting iterations
$\beta_m$ Expansion coefficient of the $m$-th basis function A scalar weight setting that function’s contribution
$b(x; \gamma_m)$ Basis function (the weak learner) A simple function characterized by $\gamma_m$
$\gamma_m$ Parameter vector of the basis function Split points and leaf values of a decision tree, for instance
$f(x)$ Final prediction function Weighted sum of all basis functions

The flexibility of the additive model lies in the choice of $b(x; \gamma)$. In different settings it takes different forms:

item.title: The Core Idea of Boosting and Its History
item.description:
The Core Idea of Boosting and Its History

Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

2.1 The core idea

The core idea of boosting fits in one sentence: combine, in sequence, a series of weak learners that are only slightly better than random guessing, and build a strong learner of arbitrarily high accuracy.

That’s a very different philosophy from bagging’s parallel voting. If bagging is many minds pulling together while staying diverse, boosting is steady, step-by-step refinement. Each round tries to correct what the previous model got wrong, concentrating on the samples that are hardest to learn. This adaptive strategy lets boosting approach the target function gradually, from simple to complex, from rough to fine.

1.1 What ensemble learning is

Ensemble learning is one of the central paradigms in machine learning, and its core idea comes from an old proverb: three cobblers working together are a match for Zhuge Liang. Statistics and machine learning formalize that idea as follows: combine several individual learners working on the same problem, and you get predictions that are more accurate and more stable than any single model can produce.

Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

Chapter 7: Cross-Modal Diffusion — Video, 3D, Audio, and Discrete Data

Diffusion models first broke through in image generation, but their core idea — starting from a simple distribution and approaching a complex data distribution through iterative denoising — is not limited to two-dimensional pixels. In recent years, researchers have extended the diffusion framework to a range of modalities, including video, three-dimensional geometry, audio, and discrete symbol sequences, creating the active frontier of cross-modal diffusion. This chapter walks through these directions one by one, focusing on three questions: what is hard about each modality, which part of the diffusion framework the main methods change, and the commonalities and trade-offs among them.

Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

Deep Learning Diffusion Models: Foundations and Classic Models

Author: ResearchWriter_基础与经典 Generated: 2026-07-02

Chapter 1: Mathematical Foundations and Core Concepts of Diffusion Models

1.1 Introduction and Historical Context

Diffusion models are one of the most important technical paradigms in generative AI today, and their theoretical roots span statistical physics, stochastic processes, and variational inference. In 2015, Sohl-Dickstein et al.1 first drew inspiration from nonequilibrium statistical mechanics and proposed a generative framework that progressively destroys data structure through a forward diffusion process and then restores it through a reverse diffusion process. Then Song & Ermon (2019)2 revisited the problem from the perspective of score matching and proposed the Noise Conditional Score Network (NCSN); Ho et al. (2020)3 developed the Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model (DDPM), which brought diffusion models into practical use through variational inference and a simplified training objective. In 2021, Song et al.4 proposed a unified framework based on stochastic differential equations (SDE), showing that NCSN and DDPM are discretizations of two classes of continuous-time diffusion processes—VE-SDE and VP-SDE—and that both can be described in the same language of “score + SDE.” In 2022, the EDM work by Karras et al.5 systematically elucidated the design space of diffusion models, unifying the choices of preconditioning, loss weighting, and samplers. This chapter starts from the mathematical foundations and systematically builds the core conceptual framework of diffusion models.

item.title: Machine Learning — Learning Theory
item.description:
Machine Learning — Learning Theory

Author: Jingmengzhiyue()

Chapter 4

Part 6: Learning Theory

1 The bias/variance tradeoff

When we discussed linear regression, we considered the following question: when fitting the data, should we choose a “simple” model such as the linear model “$y = \theta_0 +\theta_1x$”, or a “complex” model such as the polynomial “$y= \theta_0 + \theta_1x+ ...+\theta_5x^5$”? This is illustrated below:

As the rightmost plot shows, fitting with a fifth-degree polynomial does not yield a good model. Moreover, although this fifth-degree polynomial gives a very good predicted value of $y$ (the corresponding housing price) for every $x$ in the training set (for example, the living area mentioned earlier in the notes), we still cannot expect this model to give reliable predictions for points outside the training set. In other words, a model obtained by learning from the training set with a high-degree polynomial of this kind simply does not carry over to other houses. The generalization error of a hypothesis (a formal definition will be given shortly) is precisely the expected error on examples that are not necessarily in the training set.

The notes in this chapter are mainly about the support vector machine (SVM) learning algorithm. The SVM is one of the best off-the-shelf supervised learning algorithms available. Next we discuss the optimal margin classifier, which also brings in some material on Lagrange duality. We then meet kernels, which give an efficient way to carry out SVM learning in very high dimensions (for example, an infinite-dimensional space). Linear Regression

Introduction

Linear regression is a typical method among linear models.
